page: Microsoft Azure E112ibs_v5 is an isolated, memory-optimized instance engineered for demanding enterprise workloads. Built on the x86_64 architecture and managed via Microsoft Hyper-V, it provides 112 dedicated vCPUs derived from 56 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8370C processor running at a base clock speed of 2.8 GHz. The processor includes 48 KB L1 data cache, 1 MB L2 cache, and 48 MB L3 cache, alongside instruction set support for AVX-512, cryptographic acceleration via VAES and SHA-NI, and virtualization extensions. The system delivers 672.0 GB of system memory, providing 6.0 GB per vCPU. No dedicated GPUs or local storage devices are included, requiring external premium block storage for all filesystem persistence.

Benchmark data reflects strong parallel processing and memory transfer capabilities alongside moderate single-thread speeds. In multi-threaded execution, the instance achieves upper-quartile scores across stress-ng, Geekbench multi-core, and PassMark CPU metrics. Memory bandwidth is substantial, registering 5,839.55 GB/sec in cached reads and 335.8 GB/sec in uncached 256 MB reads. Accelerated cryptographic capabilities place PassMark CPU encryption scores in the top tier. Application-level evaluations reflect high throughput in data handling, recording 96.47 million operations per second in Redis SET tests and 30,672.16 in PassMark database operations. Conversely, single-core metrics across Geekbench, stress-ng, and LLM inference generation remain within average percentiles.

From an architectural standpoint, the instance balances high hardware consolidation with strict isolation guarantees. Cost efficiency is driven by high memory density and heavy parallel compute rather than burstable or small-footprint utilization. Because it lacks onboard ephemeral or scratch storage, overall deployment performance depends heavily on the provisioned network-attached block storage. The system is well structured for large-scale enterprise databases, distributed in-memory data grids, intensive ETL processing, and memory-bound computational pipelines.
